articles.label: Investigation
articles.headline: Escambia County's $2.3M Mystery Contract
articles.dek: A waste management deal approved in March still has no public work order. County staff won't say why.
brief: Escambia County commissioners approved a $2.3 million waste management contract in March 2026, but no work order or scope of services has been filed publicly
County staff have declined to answer questions about the contract's status, citing ongoing negotiations with the vendor
Public records requests filed in April remain unfulfilled past the statutory deadline
articles.body:
The contract landed on the consent agenda at 9:47 a.m. on March 12. Item 14-G. No discussion. Five yes votes. The whole thing took eleven seconds.

Three months later, no one at Escambia County will explain what the $2.3 million is actually paying for.

The approved contract, awarded to Gulf Coast Environmental Services LLC, lists "solid waste consulting and operational support" as its purpose. The term runs 24 months. Beyond that, the public record goes dark.

No scope of work. No deliverables. No timeline. No work order authorizing the vendor to begin services.

"We're still finalizing details with the contractor," said county spokeswoman Rachel Hendricks in a May 19 email. She did not respond to follow-up questions asking what details remained unfinished or why the contract was approved before those details were resolved.

The Paper Trail Stops

Under Florida's public records law, government contracts and their supporting documents must be available for inspection. Exemptions exist for active negotiations and pending litigation, but neither applies to an already-executed agreement.

The Flightline filed a public records request on April 8 seeking all documents related to the Gulf Coast Environmental Services contract, including the work order, any amendments, correspondence between county staff and the vendor, and invoices.

The statutory response window is ten business days. As of publication, 38 business days have passed. The county has provided nothing.

A second request, filed April 29, sought emails between county administrator Wes Moreno and any representative of Gulf Coast Environmental Services. That request also remains unfulfilled.

Hendricks, asked about the delays, said the records custodian's office is "working through a backlog."

A Company With Thin History

Gulf Coast Environmental Services LLC registered with the Florida Division of Corporations in November 2025, four months before securing the county contract. Its registered agent is listed as Phillip Barron of Pensacola. The company has no website and no listed phone number.

State corporate records show no prior government contracts for the company. Barron did not respond to messages left at an address associated with his name in county property records.

The company's brief existence does not automatically signal impropriety. New vendors win government contracts regularly. But the combination of a freshly formed LLC, a seven-figure contract, and missing documentation raises questions county officials have so far refused to address.

Commissioners Say They Don't Remember

Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, who voted to approve the contract, said in a phone interview he does not recall the item specifically.

"Consent agenda items are vetted by staff before they come to us," Bergosh said. "If there was a problem, it would have been flagged."

Asked whether he had reviewed the scope of work before voting, Bergosh said he relies on staff summaries for consent items. "That's how it works," he said. "We can't read every line of every contract."

Commissioner Steven Barry declined to comment. Commissioners Lumon May, Mike Kohler, and Board Chair April Olsen did not respond to interview requests.

The Money Question

County budget documents show $2.3 million allocated to "waste management services - consulting" in the fiscal year 2026 capital budget, approved last September. The line item did not specify a vendor.

Whether any funds have been disbursed to Gulf Coast Environmental Services is unknown. The county's financial transparency portal, which posts expenditures by vendor, shows no payments to the company through May 15, the most recent data available.

That could mean the contract is dormant. It could mean payments are being processed. It could mean funds are flowing through a different budget line. Without the work order and invoices the county has declined to produce, there is no way to know.

What Happens Next

Florida law provides recourse when public agencies fail to respond to records requests. Requesters can file suit in circuit court seeking compliance. If the court finds the agency unlawfully withheld records, the agency may be required to pay the requester's legal fees.

The Flightline has retained counsel and intends to file suit if the county does not produce the requested documents by June 15.

"The public has a right to know how their money is being spent," said Barbara Petersen, a former president of the First Amendment Foundation who reviewed the request denials at The Flightline's request. "A contract this size, with this little documentation, should concern every taxpayer in Escambia County."

The county commission's next regular meeting is June 10. The agenda, published May 30, contains no items related to the Gulf Coast Environmental Services contract.

Eleven seconds to approve. Three months of silence. And $2.3 million with no public accounting.

This story will be updated as new information becomes available. Tips can be sent to tips@theflightline.com.

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: Downtown's Empty Storefronts Have New Owners. Same Vacancies.
articles.dek: Palafox properties changed hands three times in 18 months. Not one has opened for business.
brief: At least seven Palafox Street storefronts have cycled through multiple owners since January 2025 without reopening
Property records show several buildings sold to out-of-state LLCs with no local business registrations
City officials say they lack tools to address speculative commercial vacancies in the downtown core
articles.body:
The storefront at 27 South Palafox has been dark for 14 months. A faded "For Lease" sign hangs crooked in the window. Dead flies line the sill. The building sold in March 2025. Then again in September. Then again in February.

Three owners in under a year. Zero tenants.

It's not alone. A Flightline review of Escambia County property records found at least seven commercial properties along Palafox Street's core blocks—between Garden and Main—have changed hands multiple times since January 2025. Not one has reopened for business.

Paper Trail, No Storefronts

The ownership trail tells a familiar story. Most recent buyers are registered LLCs based in Miami, Atlanta, or Houston. None appear in Florida's business registration database as active retailers or restaurant operators. None have filed for local business tax receipts with the city of Pensacola.

The building at 114 South Palafox, a narrow two-story that once housed a women's boutique, sold to Coastal Horizon Holdings LLC in April 2025 for $485,000. Six months later, it transferred to a related entity—Coastal Horizon II—for $610,000. The storefront remains empty. No permits have been pulled for renovation or build-out.

"It's a flip," said Marcus Treadwell, a commercial real estate broker who has worked the downtown market for 22 years. "They're not buying to operate. They're buying to sell. Or to hold until someone else pays more."

Vacancy as Strategy

The pattern isn't unique to Pensacola. Urban economists have documented similar dynamics in cities from Austin to Asheville—investors purchasing commercial properties in gentrifying downtowns with no immediate plans to lease them. The bet: rising property values will outpace the cost of carrying an empty building.

But for downtowns trying to maintain walkable retail corridors, the effect is corrosive. Empty storefronts breed more empty storefronts. Foot traffic drops. Remaining businesses struggle.

"You can have rising property values and a dying street at the same time," said Dr. Elena Voss, an urban planning professor at the University of West Florida. "The numbers look good on paper. The sidewalk tells a different story."

City's Limited Toolkit

Pensacola city officials acknowledge the problem but say their options are limited.

Florida law restricts municipalities from imposing vacancy taxes or requiring commercial property owners to actively market their spaces. The city's commercial property tax rate—among the lowest in the state—provides little financial pressure to lease.

"We can't force someone to open a business," said City Councilwoman Sherri Myers, whose district includes downtown. "We can't even force them to maintain the facade, really. Not unless it becomes a safety hazard."

The Downtown Improvement Board, a city-created taxing district, has focused its efforts on streetscaping and events rather than vacancy enforcement. Executive Director Lissa Dees said the board is "monitoring" the ownership changes but has no direct authority over property use.

"Our job is to make downtown attractive," Dees said. "What happens inside individual buildings—that's between owners and the market."

Who's Buying?

Tracing ownership of the recently flipped properties reveals a web of limited liability companies that share registered agents, mailing addresses, and—in at least two cases—identical signatories on deed transfers.

Coastal Horizon Holdings and Palafox Gateway Partners LLC share a registered agent in Coral Gables. Both entities have purchased and sold downtown Pensacola properties within the past 18 months. Neither responded to requests for comment.

A third entity, GulfPoint Commercial Acquisitions, purchased two adjacent storefronts near the Saenger Theatre in late 2025. The company's only listed officer, according to Florida Division of Corporations records, is a Nevada-based trust company that specializes in anonymous LLC formation.

Treadwell, the local broker, said he's seen the pattern before. "Out-of-state money comes in, buys everything that's not nailed down, then waits. They're not in the landlord business. They're in the asset business."

What's Lost

Walk the 100 block of South Palafox on a Tuesday afternoon. Count the doors. A vintage clothing store. A law office. A barber. Then three dark windows in a row—paper covering the glass, no signs, no indication anything is coming.

The block's foot traffic has dropped noticeably since 2024, according to Downtown Improvement Board pedestrian counts. Event weekends still draw crowds. Regular weekdays feel sparse.

Tom Nguyen ran a coffee shop on South Palafox for six years before closing in 2024. He said rising rent wasn't the only factor—it was the emptiness next door.

"People stopped walking past," Nguyen said. "When the salon closed, when the gift shop closed, nobody was coming down that stretch anymore. I couldn't survive on Gallery Night alone."

Nguyen's former space sold twice in 2025. It remains vacant.

No Easy Fix

Some cities have experimented with solutions. San Francisco imposes fees on long-term commercial vacancies. New York has considered similar measures. But such policies face legal and political resistance in Florida, where property rights carry significant weight in the state legislature.

Councilwoman Myers said she's explored whether the city could offer incentives—reduced permitting fees, expedited reviews—for owners who commit to leasing and operating retail spaces. But without state authorization to penalize vacancy, carrots may be the only available tool.

"We're competing with patience," Myers said. "These investors can afford to wait us out."

In the meantime, the storefronts stay dark. The property records keep updating. And downtown Pensacola's revival—celebrated in tourism brochures and economic development reports—remains, in some stretches, a work of careful framing.

Stand in front of 27 South Palafox. Look past the "For Lease" sign. Through the dusty glass, you can still see the outline of shelving against the back wall. Whatever business was here, it left in a hurry. Or maybe it just gave up waiting for neighbors that never came.

articles.label: Tourism
articles.headline: Blue Angels Homecoming Week Brings 200,000 Visitors. Most Won't Leave the Beach.
articles.dek: Pensacola's biggest tourism draw funnels crowds to a three-mile strip while downtown businesses wait.
brief: An estimated 200,000 visitors attended Blue Angels Homecoming Week, with the vast majority concentrated on Pensacola Beach
Downtown Pensacola businesses reported modest increases in foot traffic despite record tourism numbers
City and tourism officials are exploring shuttle programs and cross-promotional campaigns to distribute economic impact
articles.body:
The family from Atlanta had driven seven hours. They parked in the sand lot off Via de Luna, unfolded their chairs at the waterline, and watched six F/A-18 Super Hornets tear across the sky at 400 miles per hour. By 4 p.m., they were back in the car, headed to their Airbnb in Orange Beach.

They never crossed the Bob Sikes Bridge.

"We didn't even know there was a downtown," said Marcus Webb, 42, when reached by phone later that week. "We came for the show. That's it."

The Webbs are typical. Blue Angels Homecoming Week, which concluded Sunday, drew an estimated 200,000 visitors to the Pensacola area, according to Visit Pensacola. It remains the region's largest annual tourism event, a distinction it has held for decades. Hotel occupancy across Escambia and Santa Rosa counties hit 94 percent. Short-term rental bookings were up 18 percent over last year.

But the economic geography of Homecoming tells a different story than the headline numbers suggest. The crowds come. They stay on the beach. And most of them leave without spending a dollar in downtown Pensacola.

A Three-Mile Economy

Pensacola Beach stretches roughly three miles from the toll plaza to the Portofino towers. During Homecoming Week, that strip becomes one of the most densely packed tourism corridors in Northwest Florida. Casino Beach, the main viewing area for the air show, sees crowds that rival small college football stadiums.

Businesses on the island report their best week of the year. Flounder's Chowder House served over 3,000 customers on Saturday alone, according to general manager Denise Hawkins. The Sandshaker, PegLeg Pete's, and the cluster of shops along Quietwater Boardwalk all reported similar surges.

"We plan our entire year around this week," Hawkins said. "It's not even close to anything else on the calendar."

Cross the bridge into Gulf Breeze, and the picture changes. Cross another bridge into downtown Pensacola, and it changes again.

The Bridge Problem

The three-mile Bob Sikes Bridge connects Pensacola Beach to Gulf Breeze. From there, the Pensacola Bay Bridge spans another three miles to downtown. For visitors staying on the beach or in Navarre, downtown Pensacola sits on the other side of two toll bridges and 20 minutes of traffic.

Most don't bother.

"We see a bump," said Rachel Kimball, owner of Bodacious Bookstore on Palafox Street. "But it's not proportional. If 200,000 people are in town, we might get a few hundred extra customers. Maybe."

Data from the Downtown Improvement Board supports her observation. Foot traffic counters on Palafox showed a 12 percent increase during Homecoming Week compared to the same week last year. That's notable but modest given the scale of the event.

By contrast, the DIB's data from Gallery Night—a monthly event specifically designed to draw people downtown—shows 15 to 20 percent increases on those evenings.

"Homecoming doesn't move the needle for us the way you'd think," said Curt Morse, executive director of the DIB. "The beach captures that traffic. That's just the reality."

The Shuttle That Wasn't

This isn't a new problem. For at least a decade, tourism officials and downtown boosters have discussed ways to funnel Homecoming crowds across the bay.

In 2019, Visit Pensacola piloted a free shuttle service connecting Pensacola Beach to downtown during Homecoming weekend. The shuttles ran every 30 minutes from 10 a.m. to 10 p.m. Ridership was disappointing. Fewer than 400 people used the service over three days.

"People don't want to leave the beach," said Darien Schaefer, president and CEO of Visit Pensacola. "They've got their spot. They've got their cooler. They're not getting on a bus."

The shuttle program was not repeated.

Schaefer acknowledged the challenge but pushed back on framing it as a failure of tourism strategy. "Our job is to get people here. We did that. Where they spend their money once they arrive—that's a different question."

What Downtown Wants

Downtown Pensacola has transformed over the past 15 years. The Palafox corridor now features dozens of locally owned restaurants, boutiques, and bars. The Saenger Theatre and Vinyl Music Hall host national acts. The waterfront has been redeveloped with parks, a marina, and the new Hashtag development.

Business owners say they're not asking for the entire Homecoming crowd. They're asking for a slice.

"Give me 10 percent of those people," said David Bailey, owner of The District steakhouse. "Just 10 percent. That's 20,000 potential customers walking around Palafox. That would be transformational for a weekend."

Some downtown businesses have tried their own tactics. Several restaurants offered "Blue Angels specials" during Homecoming Week. The Pensacola Museum of Art extended hours and waived admission. The results were mixed.

"We had maybe a dozen people mention the special," Bailey said. "The marketing doesn't reach them. They're on the beach looking at the sky."

A Coordination Gap

The organizational structure of Homecoming itself may contribute to the disconnect. The air show is operated by the Blue Angels Foundation, a nonprofit, in coordination with Naval Air Station Pensacola. Visit Pensacola handles regional tourism marketing. The Downtown Improvement Board promotes Palafox-area businesses. Pensacola Beach is managed by the Santa Rosa Island Authority, which operates under Escambia County.

That's at least five entities with overlapping but distinct interests. Formal coordination between them on Homecoming strategy has been limited.

"There's no single table where everyone sits down and says, 'How do we maximize this for the whole region?'" Morse said. "We talk. But we don't have a unified plan."

Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose district includes Pensacola Beach, said he would support discussions about better coordination but cautioned against overengineering the event.

"The show works," Bergosh said. "People come. They have a great time. We shouldn't fix what isn't broken just because downtown wants a bigger piece."

The Numbers Behind the Numbers

Visit Pensacola estimates the total economic impact of Homecoming Week at $32 million, based on lodging, food, retail, and transportation spending. That figure has grown steadily since the Blue Angels returned to a full demonstration schedule after the pandemic.

But the distribution of that spending is uneven. The tourism bureau's own research, conducted through visitor surveys, shows that 68 percent of Homecoming visitors never venture beyond Pensacola Beach and the immediate Gulf Breeze area.

Of those who do cross into Pensacola proper, most visit NAS Pensacola for the National Naval Aviation Museum, which is free and sits on base. Relatively few make it to Palafox.

"We're talking about a funnel that gets very narrow very fast," Schaefer said.

Looking Ahead

For 2027, the Downtown Improvement Board is exploring a new approach: partnering with rideshare companies to offer discounted trips from Pensacola Beach to downtown during Homecoming weekend. The idea is to remove the friction of parking and bridge navigation that discourages visitors from making the trip.

Morse said early conversations with Uber and Lyft have been "promising but preliminary." Funding would need to come from sponsorships or the DIB's own budget.

Visit Pensacola, meanwhile, is developing a "Beyond the Beach" marketing campaign set to launch next spring. The campaign will target visitors who have already booked trips to the area, encouraging them to explore downtown attractions.

Whether any of it will work remains to be seen. The Webbs, the family from Atlanta, said they'd probably come back next year. Same routine. Same spot on the sand.

"If we wanted downtown, we'd go to Savannah," Marcus Webb said. "We came for the jets."
